content: Understanding Purpose in Life (UPL) Methodology: Interactive teaching, African proverbs, folktales, personal testimonies, peer exercises, and journaling. Discovering the Foundations of Purpose Session 1 – Introduction to Life’s Purpose (1 hour) Objective: Understand the concept of purpose and why it matters. The Story of the Three Builders: The story of the three bricklayers is based on the rebuilding of St. Paul’s Cathedral after a fire burned through London in 1666. An architect was visiting the project site and loved to interact with those doing the work and approached three bricklayers. He asked them each individually, “what are you doing?”. The first bricklayer replied, “I’m a bricklayer. I’m working hard to lay bricks to earn money so I can feed my family.” The man seemed tired and wasn’t as far along with his work as the others. The second bricklayer says, “I’m a builder. I’m building the finest, strongest wall. This wall will be a foundation for this building and will protect everyone who is inside.” The third bricklayer replied with energy and a light in his eye, “I’m a cathedral builder. I’m building a great cathedral, where people can gather, pray and celebrate the Almighty.” This is a demonstration that everything we experience is based on our understanding of purpose and depth of vision. Everything is “an inside job.” How we interpret what we do, or experience, is based on the purpose of the action and the actor, for the actor’s mindset reflects on purpose.

• Key Topics: o What is life’s purpose? 7 Questions for Clarity: 1. What makes you feel most alive? 2. What problem in the world gets you most emotionally charged? 3. What are you naturally good at? 4. What is your life’s most meaningful event or experience? 5. What would you do if you had zero fear? 6. Who is your idol, living or dead, and why? 7. What do you want to be your enduring legacy? Answer the foregoing questions sincerely, for therein lies the discovery of your purpose. o Difference between goals, vision, and purpose. 1. Purpose begets vision 2. Vision begets goals 3. Purpose: The reason for which something is done or created or for which something exists. Your purpose is the reason for your being. 4. Vision: An act or power of anticipating which will or may come to be – giving direction for the outcome of goals and purpose 5. Goals: specific, desired outcomes that guide actions and effort towards a particular predetermined end o Purpose-driven lives: Gandhi’s nonviolence, Mandela’s fight for justice, Mother Teresa’s compassion. Gandhi, Mandela and Mother Teresa are shining examples of lives well lived with purpose. Gandhi left his law practice behind and focused on liberating Asia and Africa from the yolks of colonial rule. He often took expeditions to South Africa to fellowship with the who were engaged in freedom struggle. His crown jewel of endeavor came in the form of relentless non-violent resistance against British rule of his nation, India. He summed it all in the following thought. “The main purpose of life is to live rightly, think rightly, act rightly. The soul must languish when we give all our thought to the body.” Mahatma Gandhi Mandela’s purposeful find for the liberation of his nation landed him in much trouble, and he was imprisoned and even labelled a terrorist among other things. It was his purpose that fueled his staying power. And he stayed the course until he birthed a rainbow nation out of Apartheid. “For to be free is not merely to cast off one’s chains, but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.” – Nelson Mandela

Mother Teresa’s life in Calcutta and beyond touched the world in a manner most special. Her compassion lingers on years after her demise. She did not only contribute to the assuaging of pain, but she also took part in it due to a purpose greater than herself. “Help the poor while living among them, sharing their experience and treating them with kindness, compassion and empathy, but never pity.” – Mother Teresa Napoleon Hill’s 17 Success Principles Lists Definiteness of Purpose as the top attribute in ensuring achievement. • Activity: Reflective journaling—“When did I feel most alive and fulfilled?” journalize on your personal experiences that felt, and those that feel, most meaningful.

Session 2 – The Foundations of Purpose (1.5 hours) Objective: Explore foundational principles for finding purpose. The Story of the Baobab Tree: According to https://www.oneearth.org/species-of-the- week-african-baobab-tree/ The baobab tree is a legendary plant with folktales to boot. It is known as the “tree of life” because it sustains communities through fruit, shelter, and water storage. In an arid climate, baobabs symbolize life in a landscape where little else can thrive. Its large whitish flowers open at night and fall within 24 hours, creating a beautiful display at both ends of the cycle. Here is an excerpt from One Earth: As a succulent, the tree absorbs and stores water from the rainy season in its massive trunk, producing a nutrient-dense fruit in the dry season, which can grow up to a foot long. The fruit contains tartaric acid and Vitamin C, serving as a vital nutrient and food source for many species. They are also an essential source of water and shelter for hundreds of animals, including birds, lizards, monkeys, and even elephants – which can eat their bark for moisture when there is no water nearby. Bats pollinate the flowers, feeding on their nectar. If a mere plant is created for specific value and purpose. How much more is your purpose and how much life can you sustain and support. This story edifies us that the true purpose of our life is to serve others. There are many lessons to be learned here, some of which are 1. You have a major purpose 2. You have minor purposes 3. Your minor purposes must feed into your major purpose, not out of it. 4. You discover your purpose and you discover your true life’s meaning.

• Key Topics: Napoleon Hill’s Definiteness of Purpose. Definiteness of Purpose – Your True Starting Point {Intro Video Script • Get clear – Know exactly what you want. No vague wishes—paint the picture. • Get hungry – Want it so badly it pulls you out of bed in the morning. • Get moving – Build your plan and take daily action—no excuses. • Stay locked in – Focus your mind so opportunities and resources find you. Why? Because a clear purpose gives you direction, draws the right people to you, and fuels your persistence when life gets tough. When you have it, you don’t just live life—you design it}

Napoleon Hill, one of the greatest voices in personal development, said it clearly: “Definiteness of purpose is the starting point of all achievement.” If you want to achieve anything worthwhile, this is where it begins. Let us break it down, The Success Afrika-style: 1) Know exactly what you want Don’t just say, “I want success” or “I want more money.” Those are vague wishes. Get crystal clear. Paint a vivid picture in your mind of what you want, what it looks like, feels like, and means for your life. 2) Develop a burning desire for it A definite purpose is not a casual wish you think about when it’s convenient. It’s that deep, unshakable desire that keeps you awake at night and gets you out of bed in the morning ready to move. 3) Create your game plan Once you know your target and you feel that burning desire, lay out your plan. Step by step. And keep it flexible—because life will test you, and you will need to adapt without losing sight of your goal. 4) Take consistent daily action Your definite purpose should show up in your daily calendar. Every day you do something, big or small, that moves you closer to your goal. And you do not stop until it is done. 5) Focus your mind When your mind is locked onto your purpose, something powerful happens: your subconscious starts working for you. You notice opportunities, people, and resources that you might have overlooked before. Why does this matter a great deal? 1) It gives you direction – Your purpose becomes your North Star. You always know if you’re on course or drifting. 2) It attracts resources – People, ideas, and opportunities seem to “find” you because your focus is magnetic. 3) It builds persistence – When the journey gets tough, your purpose gives you the grit to keep going until you win.

When you develop definiteness of purpose, you will no longer just live, you will move with intention. That is the difference between drifting through life and creating a life worth living. Zig Ziglar’s Wheel of Life. The Wheel of Life – Your Balance Check Zig Ziglar, one of the greatest motivators of our time, taught that life is like a wheel. If one part of the wheel is flat, your ride through life will be bumpy—no matter how fast you try to go. I like to think of it as your Life’s Balance Scorecard. There are seven key spokes in this wheel: 1. Career – Your Work & Calling Are you doing work that excites you, challenges you, and adds value to others? Your career isn’t just a paycheck—it’s part of your purpose. 2. Financial – Your Money & Resources Money isn’t everything, but it touches everything. Are you earning, saving, investing, and giving in ways that support your goals and values? 3. Spiritual – Your Faith & Inner Compass This is your core—what guides you when life gets messy. Whether through faith, meditation, or reflection, are you staying connected to your deeper “why”? 4. Physical – Your Health & Energy Your body is the vehicle that drives you through life. Are you giving it the fuel, rest, and movement it needs to perform at its best? 5. Intellectual – Your Growth & Learning If you are not growing, you are dying. Are you reading, studying, and stretching your mind so you can keep adding value to the world? 6. Family – Your Relationships at Home These are the people who know the real you. Are you investing time, love, and presence into your family relationships? 7. Social – Your Friends & Community

No one wins alone. Are you building healthy friendships, networks, and connections that inspire you and keep you accountable? Know this: If any one of the spokes is weak, the whole wheel wobbles. If several are weak, your journey slows—or stops. Balance does not mean every area is perfect all the time, but it does mean you are aware and working on them consistently. When your Wheel of Life is round and strong, you do not only survive, but you roll smoothly toward your goals – You thrive! Habits for a Meaningful Life – Og Mandino Og Mandino, one of the most inspiring authors ever, taught that a meaningful life is not built overnight, it is shaped by the habits you practice every single day. Here’s how I break down his wisdom for you: 1. Start Each Day with Gratitude Before you rush into your to-do list, pause. Name the blessings in your life—big or small. Gratitude sharpens your perspective and keeps you grounded. 2. Greet Each Day with Love in Your Heart People are your greatest resource. Approach everyone—family, colleagues, even strangers—with kindness and respect. Love opens doors that force cannot. 3. Persist Until You Succeed Challenges are not stop signs; they are detours. Keep showing up. Every failure carries a lesson, and every lesson moves you closer to your win. 4. Live Each Day as if It is Your Last Do not postpone joy, impact, or purpose. Do the thing today—make the call, take the walk, say “I love you.” Life is too short for “someday.” 5. Master Your Emotions You cannot always control what happens, but you can control your response. Stay steady when others panic and stay humble when you win. 6. Multiply Your Value Every Day

Get a little better daily—learn a skill, solve a problem, or serve someone in a new way. Growth is the fuel of a meaningful life. 7. Take Action Now: Tomorrow is not promised. Do not wait for perfect conditions. You will never have all the answers before you start. Move, and clarity will meet you along the way. The Big Picture: Og Mandino believed—and I agree—that meaningful living is not about chasing things; it is about becoming more. Practice these habits daily, and life will not just happen to you—you will be the one shaping it. • Activity: Use Zig Ziglar’s Wheel of Life to rate and reflect on different life domains. Session 3 – Purpose and Service (1 hour) Objective: See how purpose is linked to serving others. The Proverb: “When You Take the Elevator Up, Send It Back Down for Others.” This simple proverb carries a powerful life lesson: When you succeed—when you reach higher levels in life—it is not just about you. It is also about helping others climb. Let’s break it down. 1. The Elevator Up – Your Success Journey The “elevator” is whatever took you to the next level—your skills, your opportunities, your mentors, your hard work. You have moved up in life, whether in career, finances, influence, or personal growth. 2. Sending It Back Down – Creating Pathways for Others Once you are on a higher floor, do not just enjoy the view alone. Make it easier for others to rise—through mentoring, sharing knowledge, creating opportunities, or opening doors they could not open on their own. 3. Why This Matters

Because someone did it for you – Even if you worked hard, you also benefited from someone else’s guidance, time, or belief in you. Because success is sweeter when shared – True leadership is not measured by how far you go, but by how many you take with you. Because it multiplies impact – When you help one person rise, they can help others in return. My Take: Success without significance is empty. If your climb only benefits you, it is a small victory. But when you “send the elevator back down,” you turn your success into a legacy. That is how you create an impact that outlives you. I am not a mentor until I create other mentors. Wangari Maathai planted trees not for herself but for future generations. • Key Topics: Lessons from Mother Teresa – Small Acts, Big Love Mother Teresa was not famous because she held a position of power or held major bank accounts. She is remembered because she lived a life of deep compassion—proving that even the smallest acts, when done with love, can transform lives and change the world. Here is how we can bring her wisdom into our own daily lives: 1. Start Where You Are You do not need to wait for the “right time” or have a perfect plan. Mother Teresa said, “Never worry about numbers. Help one person at a time and always start with the person nearest you.” 2. See People, Not Problems She did not just see poverty, she saw people. She looked into their eyes, called them by name, and treated them with dignity. In your world, slow down enough to truly notice people. 3. Love Through Action Love is not just a feeling—it is a verb. A kind word, a listening ear, a meal shared, a hand extended. Do not underestimate the power of these moments. 4. Do Small Things Well

Mother Teresa believed that greatness is found in the quality of small acts. Fold the blanket neatly. Write the note thoughtfully. Show up on time. Excellence in small things builds trust and influence. 5. Keep Your Heart Soft The world can harden you if you let it. She chose compassion over cynicism, even in the toughest environments. Guard your heart so you can keep giving without bitterness. My Take: Big impact does not require big titles or big money. It starts with doing small things with great love—and doing them consistently. That is how you create ripples that reach farther than you will ever see. Lessons from Nelson Mandela – Unity and Justice Nelson Mandela’s life teaches us that real leadership is not about power over people, it is about bringing people together and standing for what is right, even when it costs you everything. Here is how we can live out his example: 1. Choose Unity Over Division Mandela understood that a divided nation cannot thrive. He worked to unite people across race, class, and politics. In your life, ask yourself: Am I building bridges or walls? 2. Stand Firm for Justice He spent 27 years in prison because he refused to compromise on equality. Justice sometimes demands patience, endurance, and the courage to speak truth to power—even when it is unpopular. 3. Forgive, But Do not Forget the Lesson Mandela forgave his oppressors, not to erase the past, but to create a future. Forgiveness is not weakness—it is the strength to release bitterness so progress can begin. 4. Lead With Example, Not Just Words He did not just preach unity, but he embodied it. His humility, discipline, and servant leadership made people follow him willingly. Your actions will always speak louder than your speeches. 5. See the Bigger Picture

Mandela thought beyond his own comfort and lifetime. He worked for the freedom and dignity of generations yet unborn. That is the mindset of a true leader, and it brings boundless rewards. Thought to Carry Forward: Unity and justice are not lofty ideals for history books—they are daily choices. Whether in your family, workplace, or community, you can be the one who refuses to divide, stands for what is right, and leads with integrity. When you do this, the rewards in peace of mind and material riches will always follow you. o Humility and selflessness as a foundation of service. Humility & Selflessness – The True Foundation of Service Real service is not about recognition or applause, it is about meeting needs, lifting others, and making a difference without demanding the spotlight. Humility and selflessness are the bedrock of that kind of service. 1. Put the Mission Above Your Ego When your goal is to serve, it is not about who gets the credit; it is about whether the need gets met. Focus on the mission, not on your image. 2. Listen More Than You Speak Humility starts with listening. You cannot truly serve people if you do not understand their needs. Listen with an open mind, without rushing to give answers. 3. Share the Stage Selflessness means creating space for others to shine. Give people credit for their contributions, celebrate their wins, and never be afraid to lift someone higher than yourself. 4. Serve Without Expecting Return Service is most powerful when it is unconditional. Do not keep the score or wait for favors in return. The reward is in knowing you made an impact. 5. Stay Grounded, No Matter How High You Rise Titles, positions, or wealth should never make you forget your roots. Stay approachable, relatable, and connected to the people you serve. Major Take:

Humility keeps you grounded. Selflessness keeps you focused on others. Together, they make the service pure, powerful, and transformational. When you serve this way, you do not just help people—you inspire them to serve too. • Reflection: Personal Introspection: “Who are you serving today and how?”

Session 4 – Overcoming Obstacles to Purpose. Objective: Learn how to push through internal and external challenges. Folktale: The Tortoise and the Heavy Load On a dusty African road, a tortoise carried a heavy load. The young hares mocked him, laughing at his slow pace. Yet, step by step, the tortoise whispered, “Each step, no matter how small, brings me closer to home.” By dusk, he reached his hut. His persistence turned ridicule into respect. Lesson: Purpose requires endurance. No matter how heavy the load, steady steps bring you closer to destiny. 1. Understanding Obstacles Obstacles are not interruptions of life - they are part of life. When people set out on a purposeful journey, they often expect a smooth path. Instead, they encounter resistance: critics, failures, fatigue, financial struggles, and self-doubt. These are not signs of failure; they are signs of growth. The tree that grows in gentle weather develops shallow roots, but the tree battered by storms grows deeper roots. Similarly, our obstacles create depth, resilience, and clarity. 2. Fear vs. Faith (Napoleon Hill) Napoleon Hill, in Think and Grow Rich, named six major fears that imprison people: Fear of poverty Fear of criticism Fear of ill health Fear of loss of love Fear of old age Fear of death Most people never act on purpose because these fears whisper loudly. Fear of poverty makes us settle for jobs we hate. Fear of criticism silences our voice. Fear of ill health convinces us to live small.

But Hill offered a counterforce: faith. Faith is not blind optimism. It is belief in a greater order, belief in your ability to grow, belief that adversity carries within it the seed of benefit. Fear builds walls. Faith builds bridges. Fear paralyzes. Faith mobilizes. Fear says: “what if I fail?” Faith says: “what if I learn?” Reflection: Which of Hill’s six fears has the strongest hold on you? Write it down. Then rewrite it as a faith statement. For example: “I fear criticism” becomes “I welcome feedback because it makes me sharper.” 3. Courage in Action (Gandhi) Gandhi was imprisoned multiple times. He was insulted, beaten, ridiculed. Yet, his purpose gave him courage. He transformed every obstacle into an opportunity. Prison became a podium, silence became strategy, ridicule became resilience. Courage is not the absence of fear. As Mandela said, “Courage is not the absence of fear, it’s inspiring others to move beyond it.” Courage grows when: Your vision is bigger than your fear. You see suffering not as punishment but as preparation. You act despite trembling. 4. Building Inner Clarity When you lack clarity, obstacles overwhelm you. When you have clarity, obstacles refine you. Imagine a sculptor with a rough stone. Each strike looks destructive, but slowly, the form of a masterpiece emerges. Tips to build inner clarity: Write your “why” daily. It becomes your anchor. Anchor in values. Money may disappear, applause may fade, but values endure. Reframe obstacles. Instead of asking, “Why me?” ask, “What is this teaching me?”

5. Modern Anecdotes Oprah Winfrey overcame poverty and abuse. She said: “Turn your wounds into wisdom.” Her purpose transformed pain into power. Malala Yousafzai, shot for seeking education, turned her wounds into a global movement. Obstacles often become the birthplace of the deepest callings. 6. Additional Folktale: The Lion and the Clever Hare A lion once terrorized the animals. The hare, too small to fight, used wisdom instead. He led the lion to a well, claiming another lion lived inside. The lion, seeing his own reflection, leaped in and drowned. Lesson: Obstacles are not always overcome by strength. Sometimes wisdom, strategy, and patience turn giants into shadows. 7. Activity: Resilience Journaling Step 1: Write your greatest obstacle right now. Step 2: Write the fear attached to it. Step 3: Reframe it into a faith statement. Step 4: Identify one action step you can take today. Step 5: Imagine yourself, five years from now, looking back at this obstacle. What lesson will you thank it for? Takeaway: Obstacles are not enemies of purpose: they are laboratories for transformation.

Session 5 – Practical Tools for Defining Your Purpose Objective: Craft a personal purpose statement. Anecdote: The Fisherman and the Merchant A wealthy merchant once urged a fisherman to work harder, buy more boats, and get rich. The fisherman asked, “And then what?” The merchant replied, “Then you can retire and sit by the sea.” The fisherman smiled: “But I already sit by the sea.” Lesson: True purpose is not about accumulation; it is about alignment with values and joy. 1. The Science of Purpose Psychologists call purpose a “self-organizing life aim.” It integrates goals, values, and identity. People with purpose live longer, healthier, happier lives. Purpose reduces depression, increases resilience, and boosts performance. 2. Success Afrika Techniques To uncover purpose, ask: What makes me feel most alive? What am I naturally good at? What problem makes me angry enough to act? What do others thank me for? What legacy do I want to leave? Exercise: Write answers to each question. Discuss with peers. Look for recurring themes—they point to your core purpose. 3. Identifying Passions & Strengths Purpose is not always obvious. Some discover it early; others stumble into it after decades. But you can speed the process by identifying patterns: Passion: The things that energize you. Strengths: The things you are skilled at. Needs: The problems your community faces.

Rewards: What people will support and value in you. Where these four meet lies the sweet spot of purpose. 4. Aligning with Values Values are the guardrails of purpose. Without values, purpose becomes corrupted. Consider: A gifted leader without integrity becomes a tyrant. A wealthy businessperson without compassion becomes exploitative. Purpose must serve the self and others to remain sustainable. 5. Folktale: The Hunter Who Chased Two Antelopes A hunter saw two antelopes running in opposite directions. He tried to catch both but ended with none. Lesson: Focus is essential. If your purpose is divided, you end up exhausted and empty. 6. Drafting Your Purpose Statement Framework: “The purpose of my life is to [action] so that [impact].” Examples: “The purpose of my life is to heal broken families so that communities can thrive.” “The purpose of my life is to educate girls so that nations can rise.” 7. Case Studies Nelson Mandela: His purpose: freedom and unity for South Africa. Mother Teresa: Her purpose: to serve the poorest of the poor. Wangari Maathai: Her purpose: restoring the environment and empowering women. Each purpose statement was clear, value-driven, and action-oriented.

Activity: Peer Refinement Draft your purpose statement. Share in LMS discussion forum. Receive feedback: Is it clear? Is it inspiring? Is it actionable? Refine it into one memorable sentence. Takeaway: Purpose is not found; it is defined. You do not stumble on it; you craft it.

Session 6 – Purpose in Action Objective: Integrate purpose into everyday life. Proverb: “The child who is not embraced by the village will burn it down to feel its warmth.” Lesson: Purpose thrives in connection. Without belonging, people create chaos just to be noticed. 1. Purpose in Daily Habits (Og Mandino) Og Mandino’s Greatest Salesman in the World outlines daily disciplines: Start each day with gratitude. Start every interaction with love. Persist until you succeed. Master your emotions. Multiply your value daily. These are not just habits; they are expressions of purpose. 2. Time Management for Purpose Productivity experts like Cal Newport argue that “deep work” produces the highest value. Purpose requires prioritizing what matters, not filling time with busyness. Tips: Block time for purpose-driven work. Say no to distractions that do not serve your vision. End each day with this question: Did my actions align with my purpose today? 3. Examples of Purpose in Action Wangari Maathai: She planted trees, but her deeper mission was planting hope. Strive Masiyiwa: Built Econet Wireless, but greater purpose is education. Elon Musk: Pursues space exploration, but his eyeball is on humanity’s survival.

4. African Wisdom: Ubuntu Ubuntu means “I am because we are.” It teaches that purpose cannot be lived selfishly. Your success is incomplete unless it uplifts your community. 5. Activity: Weekly Purpose Map Draw a 7-day calendar. Write your top 3 purpose-driven tasks for the week. At the end of the week, review: Did I honor my purpose? Takeaway: Purpose is not an idea to admire; it is a discipline to embody.

Session 7 – Sharing & Sustaining Your Purpose Objective: Learn how to inspire others. Anecdote: The Clay Lamp In a dark village, a clay lamp lit one, then another, until the whole village glowed. Yet the clay lamp never lost its flame. Lesson: Sharing your light multiplies it. 1. Zig Ziglar’s Principle “You can have everything you want if you help enough other people get what they want.” To multiply your purpose, share it. 2. Servant Leadership Theory Robert Greenleaf’s model: True leaders serve first. They ask, “Do those I serve grow as a people?” 3. Gandhi’s Enduring Flame Gandhi’s purpose outlived him because he lit other torches—activists, movements, nations. 4. Folktale: The Palm Tree That Shared Its Shade A palm tree grew tall but spread its leaves wide to shade villagers. Its fruit nourish, its bark shelters, and its leaves build roofs. Lesson: True greatness is measured by how many rest in your shade. 5. Activity: Community Impact Project Design a small project reflecting your purpose (mentorship, charity, teaching). Share in LMS forum. Reflect: “Whose lamp did I light?” Takeaway: Legacy is not what you achieve alone but what you ignite in others.

Session 8 – Reflection & Forward Planning Objective: Consolidate learning and set a clear future path. Allegory: The River and the Stone A river flowed over a stone for centuries. The stone mocked the river’s weakness. One day, the stone was smooth. The river whispered: “Persistence triumphs over resistance.” Lesson: Purpose shapes life not by force but by persistence. 1. Review & Refine Purpose Ask: Does my statement still resonate? Would I live this way even if no one applauded? Does it serve both me and others? 2. Strategies for Resilience Expect setbacks. Build systems: mentors, accountability, habits. Practice renewal through prayer, meditation, and rest. 3. Philosophical Insights Viktor Frankl: “Those who have a ‘why’ to live can bear almost any ‘how.’” Stoicism: External events cannot control us; only our response. African Proverbs: “When the music changes, so does the dance.” Adaptation is resilience. 4. Activities One-Year Roadmap: Write 3 goals for 30 days, 6 months, 12 months. Letter to Your Future Self: Write a letter dated one year from now. Describe how you lived your purpose. Accountability Partner: Choose one person to share your roadmap with.
Takeaway: Purpose does not end with discovery. It begins there. Reflection ensures your vision becomes a lived reality.
